newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya coffee sales up in first 5 months of season.
newsitem.headline: Kenya coffee sales up in first 5 months of season.

text.p: Kenyan coffee exports and earnings rose in the first five months of 1996/97 (October/September) as concern mounted over a shortage in global markets, coffee traders and the Coffee Board of Kenya (CBK) said on Friday.
Figures issued by the board showed Kenya exported 650,422 60-kg bags of coffee from October 1996 to around March 11, 1997, valued at around 5.69 billion shillings ($105.3 million).
That compared with 637,746 bags valued at 5.5 billion shillings in the corresponding period last year.

Figures issued by the board showed 20 export auctions were held from October to March 11, with 557,731 bags auctioned for $122.01 million. That made an overall market average of $182.30 per 50-kg bag.
Coffee is normally measured in 60-kg bags but is sold at the export auction in the capital, Nairobi, in 50-kg bags.
Total sales figures differ from auction figures because the sales figures factor in closing stocks from the previous year, normally sold and shipped in the first week of October.

Commenting on an Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC) technical meeting in London this week, a senior industry official said Kenya aimed to offload all the coffee it had because its production in 1996/97 was already too short anyway.
Key ACPC members agreed on Thursday to relax the group's export curbs in first half 1997, increasing arabica exports by 500,000 60-kg bags but leaving robusta quotas intact.
World prices for arabica coffees -- Kenya's main export -- have surged in recent months.
But Kenya has forecast that drought and an outbreak of coffee berry disease will cut its coffee production in 1996/97 to a four-year low of 78,000 tonnes.
That would compare with an earlier forecast of 85,000 tonnes and final production of 97,575 tonnes in 1995/96 and 95,806 tonnes in 1994/95.

Auction prices for some of Kenya's best quality coffees have been rising since the beginning of the year. The market has seen prices of up to $357 per 50-kg bag and the market average as at March 11 stood at $278.41 per 50-kg bag.
"Auction prices have firmed this year mainly due to tightness of supplies from producing countries and a record low stocks in consuming countries," the board said.
"Added to this is an expected smaller crop from the world's biggest producer, Brazil."

The coffee board said it was expected that coffee prices would be firm for the year as the overall global demand and supply relationship appeared to point to demand being greater than supply "at least for mild coffees".
At this week's auction, prices slipped marginally following a weak overseas market but traders remained optimistic there was enough demand to sustain the current level of high prices.
On average, prices were $20 lower than last week. The market average dropped to $253 on Tuesday compared to $278 last week.
Grades ABs averaged $271 per 50 kg compared to $291, while grade Cs averaged $251 from $278. Grade PBs averaged $272 from $293, according to CBK figures.
Prices at the auction have been upward-bound since the beginning of the year, fuelled by speculative buying ahead of an anticipated shortage in producer countries.

Traders said that despite pressure towards the downside in the world market, Kenyan coffee prices would hold -- at least until the end of July, a critical period when the market was expected to seek fresh direction following new crop figures.
Major buyers of Kenyan coffee remained Germany, the United States, the Netherlands, Belgium, Britain, Finland, Sweden, Spain, Italy, France, Switzerland, Canada, Poland and Jordan.
